rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or aggregation strategy is most informative. The entire design space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most 'null' RNA configuration. It establishes the baseline performance of RNA data with a standard, non-learned dimensionality reduction (PCA) and the simplest profile setting. This gives a clear reference point to later isolate the effect of learned encoders (scvi, scgpt), multiprofile aggregation, image modality, and fusion. 3) Why it is the best first experiment: Under a limited budget, the first experiment should be fast, interpretable, and maximally informative as a reference. PCA is computationally cheap and introduces no learned-representation confound, singleprofile eliminates the aggregation variable, and rna_only isolates the RNA signal. A strong result confirms RNA carries useful signal and sets a floor; a weak result immediately redirects attention toward image or multimodal configurations. This single experiment reduces the most uncertainty per unit of compute and provides the anchor against which every subsequent comparison (encoder choice, profile setting, modality, fusion) can be measured.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), the highest-priority uncertainty is whether the image modality adds complementary signal to RNA. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the most direct extension of config_001: it keeps the RNA encoder and profile setting identical and adds only the image branch with a simple concat fusion. This isolates the effect of adding image information with minimal confounds. If accuracy improves meaningfully over 48.5%, it confirms multimodal fusion is worth further exploration (better image encoders, fusion strategies, multiprofile). If it does not improve, it tells me the image modality (at least via resnet50) is not complementary to this RNA representation, redirecting budget toward RNA encoder quality or multiprofile aggregation. This single experiment resolves the most impactful design-axis question (model setting) before committing budget to deeper sub-axes like aggregation or fusion method.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, pca_n2000) achieved 0.485 acc, and config_016 (multimodal, pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc, a +4.2 pp gain. However, we cannot yet decompose whether this gain comes from the image modality alone or from a genuine synergistic combination. Uncertainty: We lack an image-only baseline with the same resnet50 encoder, so we cannot attribute the multimodal improvement to either modality or to interaction. This experiment (config_010: image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) isolates the image contribution by holding the image encoder and profile setting constant while removing RNA. It is the best next step because it directly decomposes the multimodal gain, informs whether further multimodal complexity (fusion variants, multiprofile aggregation) is warranted, and is a single-variable comparison to both prior experiments—maximizing information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 52.66% acc / 51.04% F1, outperforming RNA alone (config_001: 48.49%) by ~4.2 points, confirming that the weak image modality (config_010: 20.79%) still adds complementary signal. However, we have only tested one fusion strategy (concat). Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation for combining the asymmetrically-contributing RNA and image representations? config_017 is identical to config_016 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, making this a clean single-variable A/B test. Why this is the best next experiment: it directly extends our strongest configuration, isolates exactly one design decision (fusion method), and the answer will inform the fusion choice for all subsequent multimodal experiments (multiprofile, alternative encoders). Under a limited budget, resolving whether fusion strategy matters before scaling to more complex settings (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, different encoders) avoids wasting experiments on a suboptimal fusion baseline.

Evidence: The current best (config_016, multimodal/singleprofile/pca/resnet50/concat, acc 0.527) shows that RNA is the dominant signal and adding ResNet50 image features gives a modest ~4% boost over RNA-only. However, the profile axis (single vs. multi) is completely unexplored across all four experiments, representing the largest remaining uncertainty in the design space. Question: config_018 extends config_016 by switching to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000), image encoder (resnet50), and fusion (concat) constant. Because aggregation is a necessary consequence of multiprofile, this isolates a single design decision—whether multiple profiles improve the representation. Why best next experiment: If multiprofile helps, it opens the aggregation axis (avgpool vs. transformer) and confirms a promising direction for further exploitation. If it does not, we can eliminate ~30 multiprofile configurations and refocus on RNA encoder (scvi, scgpt) or image encoder (ViT-L) variations. Under a limited budget, resolving this fundamental axis is more informative than testing a secondary encoder swap that might be confounded by an unexplored profile/aggregation interaction.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) achieved the best result (acc 0.619, F1 0.610), showing a large ~9% gain over the singleprofile multimodal baseline (config_016, acc 0.527). However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) in the multiprofile setting. In the singleprofile comparison, concat vs weighted fusion made almost no difference (0.527 vs 0.523), suggesting fusion is a lower-priority axis. The aggregation mechanism is a more fundamental design choice: avgpool simply averages profile representations, while a transformer can model interactions between profiles. Question: Does transformer aggregation outperform avgpool when combining multiple profiles in a multimodal model, holding fusion=concat constant? Why this is the best next experiment: config_020 changes exactly one variable (aggregation: avgpool→transformer) relative to our current best (config_018), giving a clean isolation of the aggregation effect. If transformer helps substantially, it reveals that profile interactions are informative and justifies further investment in richer aggregation; if it does not, we confirm avgpool is sufficient and can redirect budget toward RNA encoder or image encoder choices. This is the highest-information single experiment available under the limited budget.

The strongest result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat → 0.619), which jumps ~9 points over the singleprofile multimodal baseline (0.527). However, we cannot yet decompose whether this multiprofile gain is driven primarily by better RNA aggregation (avgpool over multiple profiles) or by a synergistic interaction between multiprofile RNA and the image branch. Image-only performance is very weak (0.208), suggesting the image signal is limited, but we have no direct evidence for its marginal contribution in the multiprofile regime. config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is a clean ablation that removes only the image branch while keeping the RNA encoder, profile setting, and aggregation identical to config_018. If rna_only multiprofile approaches 0.58–0.60, the image adds little and future budget should target RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt); if it stays near 0.50, the image still contributes meaningfully and image-encoder upgrades become worthwhile. This single experiment resolves the most important architectural uncertainty and will efficiently direct all subsequent choices under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result at 0.619 acc, and RNA signal is the dominant driver (RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reaches 0.591, while image-only is only 0.208). The only RNA encoder tested so far is the simple linear PCA (pca_n2000). Question: Does a learned nonlinear RNA representation (SCVI) improve over PCA in the strongest configuration, holding all other design choices (multiprofile, avgpool, resnet50, concat) constant? Why this is the best next experiment: It isolates the RNA encoder effect in the highest-performing regime without changing multiple variables simultaneously. If SCVI improves performance, it identifies the RNA representation as a key lever for further gains; if it does not, it tells us PCA already captures the relevant variance and we should look elsewhere (e.g., image encoder or fusion). This is more informative than testing weighted fusion (config_019), where the singleprofile evidence (0.527 vs 0.523) suggests only a marginal difference, or testing a new image encoder when image-only performance is so weak that the image contribution appears limited.

Evidence: The current best config (030, multimodal/multiprofile/scvi_n200/resnet50/avgpool/concat, acc=0.632) outperforms its pca_n2000 counterpart (config_018, acc=0.619) by ~0.013, suggesting scvi_n200 may be a superior RNA encoder. However, this comparison conflates encoder quality with potential RNA-image interaction effects. Uncertainty: We lack a clean RNA-only comparison to determine whether scvi_n200 is genuinely a better representation or whether its small edge is specific to the multimodal context. Question tested: config_005 (rna_only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, avgpool) directly contrasts with config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool, acc=0.591) as a single-variable ablation of RNA encoder. Why best next experiment: This is the cleanest available isolation of the RNA encoder variable with all other factors held constant. The result will (a) confirm or refute scvi_n200 as a generally better encoder, guiding all future multimodal experiments, and (b) quantify the RNA-only ceiling so we can better attribute gains in multimodal settings to image contribution vs. encoder quality. Under a limited budget, resolving this foundational variable before further exploring image encoders or fusion strategies is the highest-information-per-experiment choice.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: The current best configuration is rna_only + scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool (0.650). Strikingly, adding resnet50 image in multimodal mode actually *hurts* performance (config_030: 0.632 vs config_005: 0.650). However, resnet50 is a weak encoder (image_only accuracy is only 0.208), so it is unclear whether the image modality is fundamentally unhelpful or whether a stronger encoder would provide complementary signal. 2) What this tests: config_036 is a clean single-variable change from config_030 (resnet50 → imagenet_vit_l), holding model_setting=multimodal, profile=multiprofile, rna_encoder=scvi_n200, aggregation=avgpool, and fusion=concat constant. It directly asks whether a much stronger visual encoder can make the image modality additive with the best RNA encoder. 3) Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget, resolving whether image has any value with scvi_n200 is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact question. A positive result opens the multimodal+ViT-L direction for further optimization; a negative result lets us confidently discard the image modality and focus remaining experiments on RNA encoder/aggregation improvements. No other single experiment reduces as much decision-relevant uncertainty.
